newsitem.title: USA: CalEnergy shocks Wall Street with NYSEG bid.
newsitem.headline: CalEnergy shocks Wall Street with NYSEG bid.

text.p: Independent power producer CalEnergy Co Inc, known for smart, aggressive transactions, surprised Wall Street on Tuesday by launching a hostile bid for a high-cost, low-growth utility that operates in a market wracked by uncertainty.

Investors and analysts say New York State Electric & Gas Corp is far less attractive than other utilities that also could provide CalEnergy with a foothold in the Northeast electricity distribution business.
NYSEG "is a very ordinary utility," said Barry Abramson of PaineWebber Inc. "It's not one of the ones that are better-situated."

Omaha, Neb.-based CalEnergy announced today it was launching a tender offer for 9.9 percent of NYSEG's shares at $24.50 each as the first step in an effort to buy the company. Further, it said it would pay $27.50 per share, or $1.9 billion, if NYSEG agreed to a friendly deal.
Analysts were skeptical that a transaction could be completed in the nine- to 12-month timeframe estimated by CalEnergy.
Utility transactions typically are long and difficult due to regulatory requirements.

Defending NYSEG as a target, CalEnergy Chief Executive David Sokol said his company could make NYSEG an aggressive competitor in an industry grappling with deregulation. NYSEG currently is battling state regulators over rates and also owns part of a high-cost nuclear plant.
"The problems that NYSEG has are...a representation of change. You've got a historically regulated monopoly business that's moving toward competition," said Sokol.
"We're very comfortable understanding what those challenges are...solving them... growing the business and going forward in a competitive way," he told analysts.

Unlike many of the transactions taking hold of corporate America, Sokol said the acquisition of NYSEG is not about consolidation and cost-cutting. CalEnergy declined to discuss the potential deal's impact on earnings, saying only that its transactions historically have been accretive.

"It seems to me an awful lot of utility mergers are...people walking two by two onto Noah's ark, just trying to avoid the flood. We think the transition to an independent marketplace is much more than just deciding whose furniture should be kept and whose furniture should be gotten rid of. The direction of this industry is very different than just trying to reduce corporate headquarters expenses," Sokol said.
Instead, CalEnergy said it was targeting NYSEG because New York will be at the forefront of states grappling with doing business in a deregulated environment.

"It will be one of the states that does move very significantly toward competition and we think that being in the middle of that process...will give us an opportunity to affect the outcome in a positive way for consumers and hopefully make it happen a little faster," he said.

But Wall Street remains unconvinced that the transaction is a sound deal for a company that last year completed a rare hostile utility takeover with its $1.3 billion bid for British utility Northern Electric Plc.
"For the life of me, I don't know why they picked NYSEG," said Ed Tirello of NatWest Securities Corp.
